units.title: Welcome and Onboarding: Start Here
units.summary: See the shape of your year, learn how each week works, and set up your portfolio so you can start strongly.

p: By the end of this welcome unit you will be able to:
Explain the aim of the year and the six pillars you will build
Describe the weekly Learning Loop and how you will be assessed
Set up your portfolio and make your first commitment to the programme

Welcome to the One-Year Life Skills Academy. Every Saturday for fifty weeks you will build the character, communication, thinking and future-readiness skills that no exam can fully measure, through true stories of young people from around the world, honest discussion and projects you actually create.

There are no high-pressure written exams here. You grow by showing up, practising, reflecting and building a portfolio of real evidence. Think of this year as a gym for life skills: you get stronger only by doing the reps.

b: Learn: build a skill each week
Lead: use it to lead yourself and serve others
Impact: prove it with a project that changes something

p: Quarter 1, Personal Excellence (Weeks 1 to 12): mindset, self-knowledge, confidence, values, goals, time, emotions, habits and resilience. It ends with the My Future Blueprint capstone.

Quarter 2, Communication and Leadership (Weeks 13 to 24): clear speaking, listening, storytelling, body language, teamwork, conflict, negotiation, service, networking and culture. It ends with The Leadership Challenge.

Quarter 3, Innovation, Thinking and Digital Readiness (Weeks 25 to 38): critical and creative thinking, problem solving, decisions, ethics, project management, leadership, AI and cyber safety. It ends with the Innovation Challenge.

Quarter 4, Career, Money and Impact (Weeks 39 to 50): financial literacy, entrepreneurship, design thinking, careers, CV and interviews, etiquette, community impact, mentoring, and your Grand Capstone.

sections.h: How each week works: the Learning Loop
p: Every unit follows the same loop, because we learn best when we experience, reflect, understand and then apply.
1. Learning goals: know what you are aiming for.
2. Warm-up and true story: connect with a real person facing a real challenge.
3. Think about it: discuss the story and what it means for you.
4. The big idea and the method: learn a clear idea and a simple step-by-step tool.
5. See it in action and common mistakes: watch the method work and avoid traps.
6. Practice lab: try it with a partner or on your own.
7. Reflect and quick check: write in your journal and test your understanding.
8. Weekly challenge: use the skill in real life and add evidence to your portfolio.

b: About 60 minutes per unit, live with a facilitator or self-paced
The quick-check questions are practice only and never count as an exam
The weekly challenge is where the real learning happens

p: Vision: to raise confident, ethical, emotionally intelligent and future-ready young people who can lead themselves, influence others positively, solve real-world problems and thrive in school, university, careers, entrepreneurship and life.
Motto: Learn. Lead. Impact.
Core values: Integrity, Respect, Responsibility, Excellence, Empathy, Courage, Innovation, Leadership, Collaboration and Lifelong Learning.
Assessment is 100% project-, portfolio- and participation-based. There is no written exam and no 100-question test bank.

Your evidence comes from four sources: weekly participation and challenges, the portfolio you build all year, three Quarterly Capstones (Weeks 12, 24 and 38) and the Grand Capstone and Summit at Week 50.
You will earn Bronze, Silver and Gold digital badges and fill in your Future Ready Passport as you go. Capstones are judged with a rubric that rewards growth, not just polish.

b: Showing up and taking part honestly
Real evidence of practice in your portfolio
Reflection: what you learned and what you will change

p: Show up on time and ready to take part; each session matters.
Respect every voice in the room. Put-downs, mockery and interrupting are not accepted in discussion or role-play.
What is shared in reflection stays in the room, unless someone's safety is at risk.
Do your own work: portfolio pieces, weekly challenges and capstone contributions must be honest efforts.
Give feedback kindly and receive it openly. Growth, not perfection, is the goal every week.
Start a folder (paper or digital) with these sections and add to it every week:
Weekly reflections
Monthly projects
Leadership activities
Presentation slides
Certificates earned
Community service record
Goal tracker
CV
Personal mission statement
Final capstone project

b: Create your portfolio folder and label each section
Write your name, your reason for joining and one thing you hope to change by Week 50
Pick an accountability partner who will check in on you each week

p: Why did I join this programme, and what do I really want from it?
What could get in the way of my showing up every Saturday, and how will I deal with it?
Which of the six pillars do I want to grow most?
The year is built around four quarters and six pillars
Each week follows the same Learning Loop: story, idea, method, practice, reflect, challenge
Assessment is through your portfolio, capstones and participation, not a written exam
Self-rating (1 to 5): How ready do I feel to start, and what will help me get to a 5?

units.title: Quarter 1 Capstone: My Future Blueprint
units.summary: Present five pieces of real evidence of who you have become since Week 1, as one coherent story.
units.warmup: In one sentence, what is the biggest thing you have realised about yourself this quarter?
goals: Combine your vision, goals, strengths, habits and growth plan into one coherent story
Present for 5 minutes with honest evidence and a believable next step
Give and receive feedback using Two Stars and a Wish
brand: Eleven Saturdays of building character, confidence and personal effectiveness lead here. This is not a test of what you can recall; it is a presentation of evidence of who you have become.

Your Blueprint has five pieces: a Personal Vision Board, your 1/5/10-year Goals (Week 6), a Strength Assessment (Week 3), a Habit Tracker (Week 10) and a Personal Growth Plan that names where you are heading next.

A strong presentation connects these into one story: a value named in Week 5, a goal set in Week 6 and a habit tracked in Week 10 should point in the same direction. That coherence is what separates real reflection from a checklist.
rubric: Evidence of honest reflection, including what has not gone well
Coherence: the five pieces point in the same direction
A believable, doable growth plan for next quarter
units.awards: Best Personal Growth, Most Improved Student, Best Reflection Journal, Best Goal Planner, Confidence Champion and the Quarter 1 Excellence Certificate
timeline: (1 min) Hook: one image or sentence from your Vision Board
(1 min) Who I was in Week 1 and what I noticed about myself
(1 min) Goals and the habit that supports them, with your tracker as proof
(1 min) A setback, what it taught you and how you responded
(1 min) Your next quarter plan and one request for help
reflect: Which of the five pieces was hardest to complete honestly?
What am I proudest of from this quarter?
What do I need to keep doing, and what do I need to stop?

check.q: What makes a Blueprint presentation strong?
o: One coherent story with honest evidence and a believable plan

check.q: Why include things that did not go well?
The awards in this quarter reward:

units.title: Quarter 2 Capstone: The Leadership Challenge
units.summary: Work as a team to solve a real community scenario under time pressure and present your response.
units.warmup: What is one thing your team is genuinely proud of building together this quarter?
goals: Divide roles early and communicate honestly as a team
Apply conflict and negotiation skills when your team disagrees
Present a specific, workable solution as one coordinated team
brand: Eleven weeks of speaking clearly, listening actively, resolving conflict, negotiating and leading through service all meet in one deliberately pressured challenge: solve a real community scenario as a team, in a set time.
Teams are judged on four things: communication, leadership, teamwork and problem-solving. Judges watch how the team works, not only whether the final solution sounds good.

Strong teams use their Team Charter from Week 18 to share roles early, and they speak up as soon as something is not working. Disagreements are expected; how the team handles them is part of the assessment.
deliver: Group presentation covering communication, leadership, teamwork and problem-solving
rubric: Communication: clear, structured, audible, everyone speaks
Leadership: roles, direction and service within the team
Problem-solving: a specific, workable solution with evidence
units.awards: Best Speaker, Outstanding Team, Emerging Leader, Best Collaboration, Creative Communicator and the Quarter 2 Excellence Certificate
timeline: (2 min) Read the scenario and agree who does what
(10 min) Define the problem, ask Why five times and list three options
(8 min) Choose one solution, plan steps, risks and backup
(5 min) Prepare a 5-minute team presentation where everyone speaks
(5 min) Present and take two questions
reflect: What role did I play, and what role should I have tried?
When did the team disagree, and how did we handle it?
What would we do differently with another hour?

check.q: What do judges look for in a team presentation?
o: Evidence of shared ownership, listening and a workable solution

check.q: Why agree roles at the start?
o: It reduces duplicated effort and gaps
It removes the need to talk

check.q: A team disagrees during the challenge. What is the best response?
o: Use calm structure such as Observe, Feel, Need, Request, and then decide together

units.title: Quarter 3 Capstone: Innovation Challenge
units.summary: Design and defend a specific, workable solution to a real-world problem using everything you practised this quarter.
units.warmup: What real-world problem, big or small, would you most like to fix?
goals: Define a real problem clearly and propose one specific solution
Show evidence of research, creativity and ethical thinking in your pitch
Pitch for 5 minutes and respond to questions with evidence
brand: Thirteen weeks of sharpening how you think, critically, creatively, ethically and digitally, lead to one test: can you design an actual, workable response to a real-world problem, not just describe it?

The Innovation Challenge draws on design thinking: a problem clearly defined (Week 25), a range of options considered (Week 26), one solution developed and defended, tested if possible with users (Weeks 27 and 41).

Strong pitches go beyond describing a problem. They commit to a specific solution, show how it could work in practice, give honest limits and consider who could be affected, using ethics (Week 29) and digital skills (Weeks 33 to 36).
rubric: Problem definition: specific, real and evidenced
Creativity and design: more than one option, one clear choice
Evidence and ethics: research, honest limits, consideration of who is affected
Pitch quality: clear story, confident delivery, strong answers to questions
units.awards: Innovation Award, Best Digital Citizen, Young Entrepreneur, Best Team Leader, Best Critical Thinker and the Quarter 3 Excellence Certificate
timeline: (30 sec) Hook: a story or a statistic about the problem
(1 min) The problem and who has it, with evidence
(1.5 min) Your solution and a prototype or sketch, and why it is better than what exists
(1 min) Evidence, risks and ethical considerations
(1 min) Next steps and what you need to make it real
reflect: How did my idea change after feedback?
Who might be affected by my solution, positively or negatively?
What would I test first if I had one more week?

check.q: What does a strong innovation pitch include?
o: A defined problem, a specific solution and evidence
A long story with no point

check.q: Why consider who could be affected by your solution?
o: A clever solution that ignores people can cause harm
